title: Pentecost
hook: a yearly renewal of openness to the Spirit
tomorrow: Jesus tells his friends to rest. why does it go wrong at once?

segments.voice: Last time, Easter kept as a whole season, with joy practiced on purpose: fifty days of joy. That season ends on a feast, and the feast starts with a noise.
screen: `FIFTY DAYS OF JOY.` → `NOW, THE FEAST AT THE END.`

segments.voice: A group chat with friends in four countries, and the translate button doing its best. Now a crowded house in Jerusalem, on a feast day. A sound from heaven, “as of a rushing mighty wind,” fills the room. Something like fire rests on each person there. They pour into the street talking, and visitors from far-off lands each hear them in their own language. Some are amazed. Some laugh and say they've been drinking. And the whole crowd asks one question: “What meaneth this?”
screen: `A RUSHING MIGHTY WIND.` → `EACH HEARS HIS OWN LANGUAGE.` → `WHAT MEANETH THIS?`

segments.voice: Peter stands up and answers. Not drunk, he says; it's far too early in the day. Pentecost was already a feast, and the city was full: “Jews, devout men, out of every nation under heaven.” This, Peter says, is what the prophet Joel promised: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams.” All flesh. Daughters as well as sons, old as well as young. And here's the detail worth telling a friend tonight: nobody had to switch languages. The Spirit didn't make everyone speak one tongue; each person heard in their own. Some readers hear an answer to Babel, where languages scattered people. Here the languages stay, and people understand anyway. So why keep a one-time morning every year? In churches that follow the Christian year, Pentecost comes back as a feast of asking again. Jesus says the Father will “give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him.” And near the Bible's last lines, the asking is one word: “And the Spirit and the bride say, Come.” Churches understand the Spirit's gifts differently; some look for tongues and healing, others for a quieter strength. The asking starts the same way.
screen: `NOT DRUNK: EVERY NATION, ONE FEAST.` · `UPON ALL FLESH.` · `NOBODY HAD TO SWITCH LANGUAGES.` · `A FEAST OF ASKING AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY, COME.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, the way you'd leave a window open for a breeze. Let each breath come in without pulling at it. If you pray, the one word from Revelation is enough, come, and then leave room.
Pentecost. The feast when the Spirit came on a crowded house, and every listener heard in their own language; kept each year as a day to ask again.
Carry this: come, one word said by the Spirit and by everyone who hears it. Day seventeen-oh-nine, done.

screen: `DAY 1709 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 28 OF 70.` → `TOMORROW: JESUS SAYS REST. WHY DOES IT GO WRONG AT ONCE?`

howItsDone: In churches that keep the Christian year, Pentecost closes the Easter season, often with red and with prayers asking the Holy Spirit to come; Pentecostal and charismatic Christians give special weight to gifts such as speaking in tongues.

Unity note: the lesson stresses Acts 2:5 ('every nation under heaven'), 'all flesh' (Acts 2:17), and that each listener heard in their own language. 'Some readers hear an answer to Babel' is hedged as a reading, not a claim about the text.
'Far too early in the day' paraphrases Acts 2:15 ('the third hour of the day'); no hour is stated in the voice.
'Pentecost comes back as a feast' is framed for churches that follow the Christian year; the range of views on the Spirit's gifts is stated without counts or ranking.
Gloss 'bride': Revelation's bride is commonly read as the church / God's people (cf. Revelation 21:9); confirm wording.
The hook's group chat with friends in four countries is a framing scene, not a claim.
